findings.title: Cache key drops accountId, enabling cross-tenant cache collisions

steps.to: user cache entries keyed without account scoping
steps.relationship: key construction drops the tenant discriminator

impactPath.limitation: Callers of userCacheKey and their cache read/write sites were not supplied; the cross-account collision outcome is inferred from the retained accountId parameter and the function's cache-key contract rather than traced in caller source.

findings.behavioralContract: A user cache key must uniquely identify cached data per tenant; the same userId under different accounts must map to distinct cache entries.
findings.failureScenario: Account A caches data for its user with userId 'u-42' under key 'u-42'. Account B later requests its own user with userId 'u-42'; the same key resolves to account A's cached entry, so account B is served account A's user data, or stale/wrong data within a single account if IDs are reused.
findings.reachability: Every cache read or write that calls userCacheKey executes the changed key construction; any userId value shared across accounts reaches the wrong cache entry.
findings.rootCause: This change removes accountId from the returned cache key, dropping tenant scoping while leaving accountId an unused parameter.
findings.impact: Cross-account cache collisions can leak one account's cached user data to another account or serve wrong data, a cross-tenant confidentiality and data-integrity defect.
findings.blastRadius: All callers of userCacheKey and every cached user-scoped value across accounts sharing userId values.
assumptions: userId values are unique only within an account, not globally
the return value is used as a cache key by callers
accountId remains a meaningful tenant identifier, since it is still a parameter
counterEvidence: If userIds are globally unique across accounts, dropping accountId is harmless; the retained unused parameter suggests per-tenant scoping, but caller code was not supplied to confirm
findings.uncertainty: Whether userId is globally unique cannot be confirmed without caller or ID-generation context.
findings.fix: Restore tenant scoping in the key, e.g. return `${accountId}:${userId}`, or remove the accountId parameter and document globally unique userIds if that is the intended contract.
findings.regressionTest: Add a unit test asserting userCacheKey('acct-1','u-1') !== userCacheKey('acct-2','u-1'); before the fix both return 'u-1' and collide, after the fix they return distinct keys.

findings.title: Dropping accountId from userCacheKey enables cross-account cache key collisions

steps.to: loadUser(accountId, userId) derives its user cache key from the changed function
steps.relationship: the supplied caller passes accountId but the changed key construction ignores it

steps.from: base key included the account scope
steps.to: distinct accounts sharing a userId now produce identical keys
steps.relationship: removing the accountId prefix collapses per-account key namespaces into one

impactPath.limitation: The cache store that consumes the returned key is not included in the supplied file or indexed context; the collision consequence is inferred from the function's name and key semantics.

findings.behavioralContract: User cache keys must be unique per (accountId, userId); lookups for two different accounts must never resolve to the same cache entry.
findings.failureScenario: Account A and Account B each contain a user with id '42'. loadUser('A','42') caches account A's user data under key '42'. A subsequent loadUser('B','42') maps to the same key and returns account A's cached user — wrong data served, stale cross-account entries, or a cross-tenant data exposure.
findings.reachability: loadUser in src/user-service.ts invokes userCacheKey for every user lookup; any userId value that repeats across accounts reaches the colliding key on the next lookup.
findings.rootCause: This change removes accountId from the key, so the returned value no longer discriminates between accounts and the per-account key namespace is collapsed.
findings.impact: Cache entries written for one account can be read by another account with the same userId, returning wrong user data and potentially exposing another tenant's user information.
findings.blastRadius: All callers of userCacheKey and every user lookup whose userId collides across accounts; existing cache entries created under the old composite key also become unreachable.
assumptions: The returned value is used as a cache key, per the function name and the loadUser call site
userId values can repeat across different accounts
The cache store is shared across accounts rather than partitioned by account
counterEvidence: If userIds are globally unique across accounts, the simplified key remains collision-free; supplied context does not establish global uniqueness
No cache read/write implementation is present in the supplied context to directly confirm the collision materializes
findings.uncertainty: Whether userId is globally unique across accounts is not established by the supplied context; if it is, the collision impact disappears.
findings.fix: Restore the account-scoped composite key (e.g. `${accountId}:${userId}`), or centralize key construction in a tenant-scoped key builder if other callers need different formats.
findings.regressionTest: Add a unit test asserting userCacheKey('accountA','u1') !== userCacheKey('accountB','u1'); before the fix the two keys are equal, after restoring the composite key they differ.

findings.title: Removed integer check lets NaN and fractional values pass port validation

steps.to: Number(value) yields NaN or a non-integer finite number (e.g. 'abc' -> NaN, '8080.5' -> 8080.5)
steps.relationship: ECMAScript Number coercion of arbitrary strings

steps.to: range check passes and parsePort returns the invalid value instead of throwing
steps.relationship: NaN comparisons are false and 8080.5 satisfies 1 <= x <= 65535; the Number.isInteger guard that rejected these was removed

impactPath.limitation: Callers of parsePort and their downstream port usage are not present in the supplied context, so end-to-end impact cannot be traced further.

findings.behavioralContract: parsePort must reject any value that is not an integer in the range 1..65535 by throwing 'invalid port'.
findings.failureScenario: A caller passes an unvalidated string such as '8080.5' or 'abc' (e.g. from an env var or CLI flag). parsePort now returns 8080.5 or NaN instead of throwing, so an invalid port reaches downstream consumers (such as a server bind or connection target) and fails there with a confusing error or misconfigures behavior.
findings.reachability: Any invocation of parsePort with a string that Number() coerces to NaN or to a non-integer within 1..65535 reaches the weakened check on every call.
findings.rootCause: The '!Number.isInteger(port)' guard was deleted from the validation condition, dropping rejection of NaN and fractional numbers.
findings.impact: Validation silently accepts NaN and fractional ports that were previously rejected, moving the failure from a clear validation error at the boundary to an opaque error or misbehavior downstream.
findings.blastRadius: All callers of parsePort in src/config.ts consumers; exact caller set is not visible in the supplied context.
assumptions: Callers rely on parsePort to reject non-integer inputs; the removal was not an intentional documented relaxation.
counterEvidence: Out-of-range values, negatives, 'Infinity', and empty strings are still rejected by the retained range check; hex and '8080.0' inputs behave as before.
If every caller independently validated integrality, impact would be reduced, but no such caller code is supplied.
findings.uncertainty: The function-level behavior change is certain; the downstream severity depends on caller handling, which was not supplied.
findings.fix: Restore the integrality guard in the condition: 'if (!Number.isInteger(port) || port < 1 || port > 65_535) {'.
findings.regressionTest: Add unit tests asserting parsePort('8080.5') and parsePort('abc') throw Error('invalid port'). Before the fix they return 8080.5 and NaN respectively; after restoring the guard they throw.
